summary.title: Toxicity of TiO2, SiO2, ZnO, CuO, Au and Ag engineered nanoparticles on hatching and early nauplii of Artemia sp
summary.authors: Ch Lakshmi N Murthy; Mohammed M Idris; Shashi Singh
summary.executive_summary: This study evaluates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three soluble salts on the hatching of Artemia cysts and the viability of early nauplii in high-salinity conditions. Using a standardized protocol involving hydrated and bleached cysts, the researchers exposed samples to concentrations of 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L. Results indicated a clear hierarchy of toxicity, with silver (Ag) and copper oxide (CuO) being the most potent, followed by zinc oxide (ZnO), gold (Au), titanium dioxide (TiO2), and finally silicon dioxide (SiO2), which showed minimal toxicity. The study established a strong inverse correlation (coefficient -0.7853) between reduced hatching rates and increased larval mortality, validating the hatching assay as a rapid, cost-effective screening tool for nanoparticle hazard identification. Mechanistic analysis via DCFDA staining revealed that silver toxicity involved reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, whereas other nanoparticles primarily caused mortality through gut clogging due to particle accumulation. The research concludes that Artemia sp. is a robust model organism for assessing nanomaterial risks in aquatic environments, offering a high-throughput alternative to traditional long-term toxicity assays.

Executive Summary
This study evaluates the acute toxicity of six engineered nanoparticles (Ag, Au, CuO, ZnO, TiO2, SiO2) and three soluble salts on the hatching of Artemia cysts and the viability of early nauplii in high-salinity conditions. Using a standardized protocol involving hydrated and bleached cysts, the researchers exposed samples to concentrations of 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L. Results indicated a clear hierarchy of toxicity, with silver (Ag) and copper oxide (CuO) being the most potent, followed by zinc oxide (ZnO), gold (Au), titanium dioxide (TiO2), and finally silicon dioxide (SiO2), which showed minimal toxicity. The study established a strong inverse correlation (coefficient -0.7853) between reduced hatching rates and increased larval mortality, validating the hatching assay as a rapid, cost-effective screening tool for nanoparticle hazard identification. Mechanistic analysis via DCFDA staining revealed that silver toxicity involved reactive oxygen species (ROS) generation, whereas other nanoparticles primarily caused mortality through gut clogging due to particle accumulation. The research concludes that Artemia sp. is a robust model organism for assessing nanomaterial risks in aquatic environments, offering a high-throughput alternative to traditional long-term toxicity assays.

Research Context
Nanomaterials pose significant risks to aquatic ecosystems due to their unique physicochemical properties. There is a critical lack of information regarding the bioavailability and biopersistence of nanoscale objects. Existing ecotoxicology assays often rely on complex models like fish or Daphnia, lacking high-throughput options.

Research Question And Hypothesis
The study aims to determine the relative toxicity order of various engineered nanoparticles on Artemia development. It is hypothesized that hatching rates of cysts will inversely correlate with the mortality of hatched nauplii. The researchers predict that silver and copper oxide will exhibit the highest toxicity compared to metal oxides and silicon. The study seeks to validate the hatching assay as a reliable proxy for standard larval toxicity tests.

Methodological Details
Six engineered nanoparticles and three soluble salts were tested against Artemia sp. Nanoparticles were sourced from the NANOVALID consortium or synthesized in-house. Artemia cysts were hydrated for 45 minutes and bleached with 20% sodium hypochlorite for 15 minutes. Experiments were conducted in 25% salt water at pH 8.0 and 28°C with continuous aeration. Two concentrations, 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L, were used for the hatching rate experiments. Hatching was monitored for 24 hours, counting motile vs. immotile nauplii and unhatched cysts. A standard toxicity test exposed nauplii to five concentrations ranging from 100 mg/L down to 0.01 mg/L. Viability was assessed every 6 hours up to 48 hours by observing cessation of swimming. Oxidative stress was measured using 10µM DCFDA staining and fluorescence microscopy. Statistical analysis was performed using Graphpad software to calculate LD50 and correlation coefficients.

Procedures And Architectures
Nanoparticle suspensions were sonicated at ~30W with a 50% pulse for 10 minutes. Characterization included TEM on formvar coated copper grids and DLS using Horiba Nanopartica SZ100. TEM analysis was conducted at 100KV using a 20µ aperture and GATAN camera software. DLS measurements were performed in triplicate over three days in both MilliQ and salt water. The hatching assay utilized a continuous aeration system to keep particles in suspension. The standard toxicity test followed the ARC (Artemia Reference Centre) protocol using six-well plates. Nauplii were not fed during the 48-hour test period to isolate toxicity effects. Gut accumulation was visualized by examining the digestive tract of dead and live nauplii. ROS and superoxide levels were detected using DCFDA and DHE fluorescent stains respectively.

Key Results
The established toxicity order was Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2 based on hatching inhibition. At 100 mg/L, silver and copper oxide reduced hatching rates to approximately 29%. Silver nanoparticles at 10 mg/L reduced hatching to lower levels but maintained 85% viability. Copper oxide at 10 mg/L showed low hatching rates with around 64% viability. Gold and silicon dioxide nanoparticles displayed very good viability after hatching. Silicon dioxide at 10 mg/L showed hatching and viability equivalent to the controls. Silver nitrate (ionic form) caused 80% mortality in nauplii within 24 hours. The LC50 for silver nanoparticles was calculated to be around 10.12 mg/L at 24 hours. A strong inverse correlation with a coefficient of -0.7853 was found between hatching rates and larval mortality. No statistically significant difference was found between viability in ARC test and hatching rate (P=0.683). DCFDA staining revealed ROS accumulation in nauplii exposed to silver, titania, and silicon. Other nanoparticles caused mortality primarily through gut clogging rather than ROS generation.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
Silver toxicity is driven by ionic release and ROS generation, unlike other nanoparticles. The hatching assay serves as a valid high-throughput screening tool for nanoparticle hazard identification. Artemia sp. is a suitable model organism due to its filter-feeding nature and tolerance to salinity. The study confirms that reduced hatching rates effectively predict subsequent larval mortality. Continuous aeration in the hatching test prevents sedimentation, ensuring consistent particle exposure. Gut accumulation of nanoparticles is a primary mechanism of mortality for non-ionic particles.

Contradictions And Limitations
The study lacks detailed demographic data on the specific Artemia strain beyond 'San Francisco Bay strain'. The study notes that silicon nanoparticles at low concentrations were conducive, showing better hatching than control. Flocculation and sedimentation of copper and zinc oxide nanoparticles may affect exposure consistency over time.

Both the tests show good inverse correlation in sensitivity to nanoparticles The correlation test showed a coefficient of -0.7853 Comparing the viability of nauplii in ARC test with the hatching rate showed no statistically significant difference These acute toxicity tests eliminate the need of laboratory maintenance of test species that take up space and time

Robustness And Ablation Notes
The experiment was repeated six times to ensure validity and calculate SEM. Validity was confirmed by low mortality in control groups below 10% in 24 hours.

Ethical Considerations
The study uses Artemia sp., a non-selective filter feeder, which is considered a good model organism.

Key Figures Tables
Table 1 presents the hatching rates and viability percentages for all tested nanoparticles at 100 mg/L and 10 mg/L. Figure 3 illustrates the drastic alteration in hatching rates in the presence of nanoparticles. Figure 4 shows the mortality curves and LC50 values for the standard toxicity test. Figure 5 displays the accumulation of nanoparticles in the gut of Artemia nauplii. Figure 6 demonstrates the strong inverse correlation between hatching rates and larval mortality.

Three Takeaways
1. The core contribution is the establishment of a toxicity hierarchy: Ag>CuO>ZnO>Au>TiO2>SiO2. 2. The strongest evidence is the inverse correlation coefficient of -0.7853 between hatching and mortality. 3. The future path involves adopting Artemia hatchability tests as high-throughput pre-screening tools.
